notes:
I found no sharp disagreements between Protestant denominations on Psalm 101. The real splits are between individual commentators: whether the psalm is about public office or private life, how to read "when will You come to me?" in v. 2, and whether v. 4 is about David's own heart or about wicked people. I didn't find anything from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org (Orthodox), or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, so those are left out. My searches and page reads ran out before I could reach them.

**The psalm as a whole**
- It became known as the "prince's Psalm." Luther's version heads it "David's mirror of a monarch". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-8.htm
- Boice, quoted by Guzik, says Luther wrote an 80-page exposition of it because he was deeply concerned about civil government. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-101/
- Matthew Henry says it doesn't matter exactly when it was written. It is a model for a royal court, but it is applicable to private families; it is the householder's psalm. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_101.cfm
- Modern-critical note: Keil and Delitzsch accept David as author. They suggest a source used by the Chronicler gave a later, post-exilic collector a further gleaning of Davidic songs, or at least songs that were ascribed to David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-8.htm

**v. 1**
- Guzik: mercy and justice belong together. Before he could exercise mercy and justice in His kingdom, he had to understand and extol the mercy and justice of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-101/
- Spurgeon: David praises both God's love and God's severity, and there is as much love in the blows of his hand as in the kisses of his mouth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-1.htm
- Barnes: David praises these virtues best by practising them. A father or magistrate is but the representative of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-1.htm
- Ellicott: mercy and justice are the especially requisite attributes of a good monarch, or of magistrates generally. https://biblehub.com/psalms/101-1.htm
- Gill offers two readings. Either it is David's own mercy and justice as ruler, or rather of the mercy of God to himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/101-1.html
- The Sermon Bible says mercy and justice union takes place in Christ crucified. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/sermon/psalms/101.htm
- **Where readings differ:** Augustine (Catholic) reads the word order as a timeline: the present is the season for mercy, the future for judgment. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801101.htm. Calvin (Reformed) takes the verse as a vow to be a just king. He calls Augustine's reading too refined. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_101_1-5.htm
- Haydock (Catholic) calls mercy and judgment the chief qualifications of a king. Citing Jerome and Augustine, he says no one should presume, because there is judgment, and no one should despair, because mercy comes first. https://studylight.org/commentaries/hcc/psalms-100.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: under the Old Covenant blessing, including the experience of God's presence, was connected to obedience. David's integrity had to be real at home before it could be real at court. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-101/
- Spurgeon: What we are at home, that we are indeed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-1.htm
- **"When will You come to me?"** is read in several ways:
  - Spurgeon: David longs for God's presence so he will be fit to reign. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-101/
  - Barnes: better rendered "when thou dost come." Whenever God visits, He will always find these principles at work in David's house.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-2.htm
  - Ellicott calls a link to the ark story (2 Sam 6:9) far-fetched. He suggests the subject is the "perfect way" itself: whenever a choice between right and wrong comes to him, he will choose the better.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-2.htm
  - Keil and Delitzsch keep it as a question: a question of strong yearning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-8.htm
  - Calvin prefers "till Thou comest." Even before he held royal power, while still a private man, David kept to uprightness. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_101_1-5.htm
- Augustine: the "midst of my house" means either the Church or one's own heart. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801101.htm

**v. 3**
- Spurgeon: I will neither delight in it, aim at it or endure it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps101.cfm
- Guzik links the verse to the lust of the eyes and Job 31:1. He notes David later failed this very standard with Bathsheba.  But it isn't hypocrisy to have a standard that you can't completely meet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-101/
- Ellicott: the vow is wise for a despotic king, who only has to speak to get whatever he looks at with desire. The Hebrew is literally "thing of Belial."  https://biblehub.com/psalms/101-3.htm
- Matthew Henry: David will never aim to enrich himself by impoverishing his subjects. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/101-1.html
- On "those who fall away": Boice (via Guzik) says it is the exact opposite of the covenant love (*hesed*) of v. 1. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-101/
- Barnes: the phrase means wanderers from the right path, and a wicked plan tends to stick to a person like pitch or wax.  Gill applies it to apostasy from the gospel (Heb 10:38). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-3.htm
- Calvin: to set a wicked thing before one's eyes means to plan to do it. Only someone who hates wrongdoing can punish it fairly. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_101_1-5.htm
- Augustine: hate the unfaithfulness, not the person. God made the man; the man made himself unfaithful. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801101.htm

**v. 4**
- **Self or others?**
  - Barnes says the verse could mean either David's own conduct or the people who work for him.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-101.html
  - Benson reads it as wicked men put out of the court. "I will not know" means he will not support or approve them.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-3.htm
  - Calvin rejects reading "perverse heart" as wicked men. He calls that too forced, and says David is promising to keep himself free from wrongdoing. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_101_1-5.htm
- Kidner (via Guzik) describes the perverseness as deliberate, a twisted mind that hates the straight path. Chandler compares it to an unruly horse champing at the bit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-101/
- Clarke: I will cultivate no acquaintance with them. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/psalms/101-8.html
- Augustine: "know" here means "approve," as in Matthew 7:23, "I never knew you." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801101.htm

**v. 5**
- Gill and Clarke (via Guzik) mention the Jewish idea of the "triple tongue." Slander kills three persons; him that carries the slander, him that receives it, and him of whom it is related. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-5.htm
- Barnes: "cut off" means I will not employ him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-5.htm
- Benson: these are informers trying to advance themselves by the ruin of others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-5.htm
- Another commentator on the same page (not named in the excerpt) links this to David's own experience of tale-bearers under Saul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-5.htm
- **Public office or private life?** Calvin says this verse is about the duty of a king who bears the sword. Private believers do not have the right to cut off slanderers. He says David, while still a private man, never tried any such thing. He also explains "wide of heart" as insatiable ambition. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_101_1-5.htm
- Spurgeon makes the same distinction: the office of the magistrate is of another kind from that of private Christians, who are called to be patient and kind. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps101.cfm
- Augustine: the righteous persecutor, not of the man, but of the sin. That line is in the New Advent search excerpt, and the full text shows it in his comment on v. 5. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801101.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik: character matters more than competence.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-101/
- Matthew Henry: Saul chose servants for their goodliness, but David chose them for their goodness. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_101.cfm
- Constable: Professional competence was not sufficient to qualify a member of David's staff for service. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/101-8.html
- Pulpit Commentary: "my eyes" means my favour shall be shown to them. Gill reads it of Christ's eyes on faithful ministers and church members. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-6.htm
- Calvin: servants are the "hands of a prince." A good king with corrupt officers is of little use to his people. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_101_6-8.htm
- Augustine (Latin text "sit with me") links it to the faithful who will sit on thrones in judgment (Matt 19:28).  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801101.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: "stand in my presence" means to stand as a courtier in theroyal presence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-101.html
- Barnes: even if a liar gets into the house, he will not stay. He will be dismissed once his character is known.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-7.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: a king must see that his whole household is righteous, and the liar shall not keep his position in my court. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-7.htm
- Gill applies the verse to hypocrites and false teachers, who will have no place in Christ's house. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-7.htm
- Calvin: this is about those closest to the king. Someone who cannot keep order in his own house is not fit to govern a kingdom. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_101_6-8.htm

**v. 8**
- "Every morning" probably refers to the custom of holding courts of law in the early morning (Ellicott, following Perowne). https://biblehub.com/psalms/101-8.htm
- Barnes: it would be his first task each day, morning by morning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-8.htm
- Calvin: rulers must stop evil early, but without anger or haste. Since David could not purge the land completely, he is really promising to judge fairly whatever a person's rank.  In the full text, Calvin also points ahead to Christ, who will one day separate the sheep from the goats. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_4/psalm_101_6-8.htm
- Pulpit Commentary appeals to Romans 13:4. It warns against a weak and over-indulgent ruler, and notes the capital always attracts the criminal classes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-8.htm
- Matthew Henry looks ahead to that future, most awful morning of final judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/101-8.htm
- Coffman: David's hopes along this line were never completely achieved. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/101-8.html
- Augustine: the wicked are spared now because it is "night," the season of mercy. At dawn, meaning the Judgment, Christ shall slay them at the dawn, and shall destroy them from His city. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801101.htm
- Haydock (Catholic): The Fathers admonish us to resist temptations at the beginning. https://studylight.org/commentaries/hcc/psalms-100.html
